title: Motives and Means — The Age of Exploration, Chapter 2
eyebrow: CKHG Grade 5 · The Age of Exploration · Chapter 2 · Student Reader pp. 10–17
bigQuestion: What developments enabled Europeans to travel farther?

missions.name: Motives and Means
missions.blurb: One quiz for the whole chapter, with questions from each of its four headed sections and the Big Question at the end. Mostly what happened; a few on the words the chapter is built from. The card says which page answers it, and a wrong answer opens that page.

hi: several motives for exploration
the monopoly held by Arab traders

vs.q: The chapter says Europeans had several motives for exploration. What is a motive?
opts: The reason for taking a specific action
A map of a route nobody has sailed
An order given by a king to a captain
A share of the profit from a voyage
vs.why: A reason for doing something. The chapter's title is Motives and Means: the motives are why Europeans wanted to go, the means are what finally let them.

vs.q: Why were spices so valuable throughout Europe?
opts: Arab traders and Venetian merchants held a monopoly
The plants would only grow on one small island
European rulers had banned all but a few of them
They had to be ground by hand before they were sold
vs.why: The same monopoly from chapter 1. Anyone in Europe who wanted spices had to buy them from people who could name their own price.

hi: direct access to the spice-growing areas
peppercorns were used in place of coins

vs.q: What does the chapter name as one of the Europeans' motives?
opts: Direct access to the spice-growing areas
Finding new land to farm for their kings
Spreading the Crusades into Asia
Catching up with Chinese shipbuilders
vs.why: They wanted to reach the spice-growing areas themselves, the ones Marco Polo had described, instead of buying through the Arabs and the Venetians.

vs.q: In some places, spices were so valuable that peppercorns were used in place of what?
opts: Coins
Medicine
Salt
Seeds
vs.why: Money. Payments were counted out peppercorn by peppercorn, and spices by the pound paid fees, taxes, rents and ransoms.

hi: their food was not very tasty
to cure the meat for long-term storage

vs.q: Why were Europeans so enthusiastic about spices?
opts: Their food was not very tasty
Their doctors said spices cured illness
Their religion asked them to eat spices
Their rulers gave spices out as gifts
vs.why: No potatoes, tomatoes, corn, bananas, chocolate, peanuts or pineapples, no sugar until late in the Middle Ages, and no coffee or tea. A pinch of pepper made a great deal of difference.

vs.q: Europeans used salt to cure meat. What does cure mean here?
opts: To preserve food by smoking, drying, or salting it
To make somebody well again after an illness
To cook meat slowly over a very low fire
To trade meat for something else of value
vs.why: Not curing an illness — curing food. Livestock was butchered in the fall and salted to keep, and after a few months it needed all the pepper and cloves it could get.

hi: The Turks shut down the Silk Road
needed a sea route to Asia

vs.q: What happened in the fifteenth century that made getting spices even harder?
opts: The Turks shut down the Silk Road
The Arabs stopped sailing to the islands
Venice refused to sell to northern Europe
A storm destroyed the Venetian fleet
vs.why: The Silk Road was the land route spices had come along from the East. With it closed, the overland way was gone.

vs.q: Once the land route was closed, what did Europeans need?
opts: A sea route to Asia
A treaty with the Turks
A new spice to grow at home
A larger army in the Middle East
vs.why: Nobody was sure a sea route even existed. The great kings of Europe started looking for explorers, shipbuilders and mapmakers who could find one.

hi: much more advanced than they had been led to believe
described the goods and cultures they had encountered

vs.q: What did Europeans find when they reached the Middle East on the Crusades?
opts: Islamic civilization was more advanced than they thought
The Holy Land had already been abandoned
The spice trade was being run from there
Their own ships were already the best in the whole world
vs.why: They had been led to believe otherwise. Seeing it for themselves is what changed things.

vs.q: How did the Crusades help fuel exploration?
opts: Crusaders came home describing what they had seen
Crusaders brought back maps of all of Asia
Crusaders captured ships that could cross oceans
The pope ordered Europe to find a route east
vs.why: Curiosity. Knights and soldiers came home talking about what was out there, and that added to European interest in the world beyond their borders.

hi: a great deal about navigation and shipbuilding
long voyages across uncharted waters

vs.q: What is navigation?
opts: Planning and directing the movement of a ship
Building a ship strong enough for rough seas
Loading a ship so that it sits level in the water
Drawing the coastline of a country onto a map
vs.why: Working out where you are and steering where you mean to go. Arab traders had centuries of it; Europeans, at this point, did not.

vs.q: The book says European ships could not manage uncharted waters. What does uncharted mean?
opts: Never mapped
Too shallow to sail
Claimed by another country
Far from any trade route
vs.why: No chart, no map. Sailing water nobody had mapped is a different thing from sailing a coast you know, and European ships were built for the second.

hi: staying near the coastline and watching for known landmarks
not well-suited to long voyages

vs.q: How did European sailors usually find their way at this time?
opts: By staying near the coast and watching for landmarks
By following the Arab traders' ships at a distance
By using the magnetic compass on every voyage
By counting the days since they had left port
vs.why: Short voyages in European waters, always in sight of something they recognised. That works until you lose sight of land.

vs.q: What does the chapter say European ships were not well-suited to?
opts: Long voyages across uncharted waters
Carrying heavy loads of trade goods
Sailing in the warm Mediterranean
Being handled by a very small crew
vs.why: Their skills were behind their competitors' and their ships were built for something else. Both had to change before anyone could sail to Asia.

hi: large triangular sails, called lateen sails
hulls built with thick, overlapping planks

vs.q: What kind of sails did ships built in southern Europe have?
opts: Large triangular sails, called lateen sails
Small square sails set low on the mast
Round sails that could be turned by hand
Two short sails, one behind the other
vs.why: Lateen sails, which handled easily in the winds along the Mediterranean coast. Northern ships had square sails instead, better on the open ocean.

vs.q: What is a ship's hull?
opts: The sides and bottom of a boat
The deck a crew walks about on
The mast the sails are hung from
The rope that holds the anchor
vs.why: The body of the boat. Northern ships built theirs from thick, overlapping planks to stand up to the Baltic and the Atlantic.

hi: Portuguese shipbuilders combined features
the sturdiness of the northern ships

vs.q: What was a caravel?
opts: A ship with northern sturdiness and southern handling
A ship rowed by many men as well as being sailed
A ship built only to carry spices home
A ship with no deck, for shallow water
vs.why: The best of both designs in one hull, with lateen sails for easy handling and square sails for the open ocean. This is the chapter's great means.

vs.q: Who combined the two kinds of ship to make the caravel?
opts: Portuguese shipbuilders
Venetian merchants
Arab traders
English sailors
vs.why: Portuguese shipbuilders, in the 1400s. It is worth remembering, because the next chapter is about where Portugal then sailed.

hi: the astrolabe and later the sextant
they relied on the sky

vs.q: What is an astrolabe?
opts: A tool for finding the position of the sun or a star
A glass device that measures the passing of time
A pointer that always swings towards the north
A rope with knots tied along it at even spaces
vs.why: It measures how high the sun, moon or a star sits in the sky. The other three answers are the hourglass, the compass and the log line — all in this chapter too.

vs.q: What is a sextant?
opts: An instrument with a telescope, for finding latitude
A chart showing the depth of a harbor
A sail that can only be raised in a strong wind
A lamp hung at the top of a ship's mast
vs.why: A later and better instrument than the astrolabe, using a telescope and a scale to work out latitude and longitude.

hi: to determine the ship's latitude
the sun's apparent movement across the sky from east to west

vs.q: What did ship pilots use the astrolabe and the sextant to work out?
opts: The ship's latitude
The ship's speed
The depth of the water
The strength of the wind
vs.why: How far north or south they were. They measured the height of the sun, moon and stars to get it — difficult on a bobbing ship.

vs.q: During the day, how could sailors tell which direction they were heading?
opts: From the sun's movement across the sky
From the direction the waves were running
From the colour of the water around them
From the way the sails filled with wind
vs.why: The sun crosses from east to west, so the sun setting on the right of the ship meant the ship was heading south.

hi: Speed was measured using a log attached to a rope
The magnetic compass , a Chinese invention

vs.q: How was a ship's speed measured?
opts: By counting knots on a rope let out behind the ship
By timing how long the ship took to pass an island
By watching how fast the sand ran in the hourglass
By measuring how deep the ship sat in the water
vs.why: A log on a knotted rope. A sailor counted the knots slipping through his hands, and ship speed is still measured in knots today.

vs.q: Where was the magnetic compass invented?
opts: China
Portugal
Arabia
Venice
vs.why: A Chinese invention, already centuries old. Europeans used it to find direction, though the chapter says many captains did not understand how it worked.

hi: building new ships, learning more about navigation, and updating their maps
observations made by the crew

vs.q: What developments enabled Europeans to travel farther?
opts: New ships, better navigation, and updated maps
Bigger crews and more food on board
Peace with the Turks and the Arab traders
Larger harbors along the European coast
vs.why: This is the chapter's Big Question, and the last paragraph answers it in one line. The caravel, the astrolabe, the compass and the hourglass are the means the title promised.

vs.q: Besides instruments, what else did navigators use to work out where they were?
opts: What the crew noticed around the ship
Letters sent ahead to the next port
The number of days since leaving home
Signals from other ships nearby
vs.why: Clouds, birds, waves and anything floating in the water. Put all of it together with new ships and new instruments and Europeans could finally think about sailing to far-flung parts of the world.

value.title: The Value of Spices — why anyone bothered
vocab: the reason for taking a specific action
text: By the mid-1400s, Europeans had several motives for exploration. For one thing, they wanted direct access to the spice-growing areas of the world described by Marco Polo.

Because of the monopoly held by Arab traders and Venetian merchants, spices were very valuable throughout Europe. In some places, spices were so valuable that peppercorns were used in place of coins. Payments were even counted out peppercorn by peppercorn.

food.title: The Value of Spices — what Europeans were eating
vocab: to preserve meat, fish, or other food by smoking, drying, or salting it
text: Europeans were so enthusiastic about spices because their food was not very tasty. At this time Europeans did not yet have any of the fruits and vegetables native to North and South America. Potatoes, tomatoes, corn, bananas, chocolate, peanuts, strawberries, blueberries, and pineapples were all unheard of.

Europeans typically butchered livestock in the fall. They used salt to cure the meat for long-term storage. After a few months, much of this meat was not very appetizing. A pinch of pepper, cloves, or ginger could make bad tasting or even spoiled meat much easier to eat.

silkroad.title: The Value of Spices — the land route closes
text: Then, in the fifteenth century, the quest for spices became even more problematic. The Turks shut down the Silk Road, an important land route, which had previously been used to transport spices from the East.

The Europeans needed a sea route to Asia. Nobody was sure that such a route existed. Everybody hoped one would be discovered. The great kings of Europe began looking for brave explorers, shipbuilders, mapmakers, and others who could help them with this quest.

crusades.title: The Crusades — what the soldiers saw
text: Exploration was also fueled by another series of events. In the Middle Ages, generations of European knights and soldiers went on Crusades to the Middle East to capture the Holy Land from Muslims.

When Europeans reached the Middle East, they saw that Islamic civilization was much more advanced than they had been led to believe. Crusaders returned home and described the goods and cultures they had encountered. This added to European curiosity about the world outside their borders.

ships.title: New Ships — what Europe had to start with
vocab: the act of planning and directing the movement of a ship, plane, or other vehicle
the sides and bottom of a boat
text: Arab traders had been sailing across the Indian Ocean for centuries. Therefore, they had learned a great deal about navigation and shipbuilding. By comparison, Europeans generally made shorter voyages within European waters. European sailors navigated mostly by staying near the coastline and watching for known landmarks.
Their navigational skills were not as advanced as their competitors'. Their ships were not well-suited to long voyages across uncharted waters.

Generally, ships built in the Mediterranean shipyards of southern Europe had large triangular sails, called lateen sails . These sails provided easy handling in the winds that blew along the Mediterranean coast. Northern ships had square sails, which were more effective on the open ocean. They also had hulls built with thick, overlapping planks. These hulls were built to withstand the rougher waters of the Baltic Sea and the Atlantic Ocean.

caravel.title: New Ships — the caravel
text: Both of these ship designs had advantages, but neither was ideal for long voyages on uncharted waters. Then, in the 1400s, Portuguese shipbuilders combined features from these two different kinds of ships. By doing this, they created new, more seaworthy vessels called caravels

Caravels had the sturdiness of the northern ships and the easy handling of the southern ships. Their masts were rigged with lateen sails so that the ships were easy to handle, but the caravels also had square sails to take advantage of strong winds that could send the ships across the open ocean. The ships had hulls sturdy enough to sail on rough seas.

sky.title: Finding Their Way — steering by the sky
vocab: a navigational tool used to determine the position of the sun, a star, or other object in the sky
a navigational instrument that uses a telescope and scale to determine latitude and longitude
text: Sailors needed ways to keep track of their location and direction when they were out of sight of land. To do this, they relied on the sky.

During the day, sailors could plot their direction in relation to the sun's apparent movement across the sky from east to west. For example, the sun setting on the right side of the ship would mean that the ship was heading south.
Ship pilots also had a variety of navigational tools to help keep their ships on course. Pilots used instruments such as the astrolabe and later the sextant to determine the ship's latitude.

tools.title: Finding Their Way — speed, and direction
vocab: a device that uses a magnetized pointer to show direction
text: Speed was measured using a log attached to a rope. The rope had knots tied along it at regular spaces. A sailor counted the knots as they slipped through his hands. The number of knots let out during a certain amount of time was used to calculate the speed. Today, ship speed is still measured in knots.
The magnetic compass , a Chinese invention, had been in use in other parts of the world for centuries. Europeans also relied on it to determine direction.

ends.title: Finding Their Way — time, and what it all added up to
vocab: a glass device that measures time using the flow of sand
text: To measure the passage of time, sailors used a sand hourglass. The ship's cabin boy turned the glass every half hour.
Navigators also made use of observations made by the crew. Information about the clouds, birds, waves, and anything floating in the water all helped to track a ship's position on the sea.
Europeans were building new ships, learning more about navigation, and updating their maps. Soon, they might really be able to sail to far-flung parts of the world.
